guidance.procedure: Locate every operative confidentiality definition and identification condition before deciding. For technical-only coverage, determine whether the protected class is actually confined to technical matter; business, financial, commercial, customer, or marketing coverage opposes exclusivity, while an illustrative technical list does not establish exclusivity unless its scope is closed. Explicit identification requires marking or designation as a condition for all protected information; reasonable-person or regardless-of-label coverage opposes it. For oral or visual information, preserve contemporaneous designation and later written-confirmation requirements. Cite the complete grammatical chain and independently operative repeated definitions; exclude titles, recitals, exclusions, and neighboring categories that do not supply scope.

Run three separate lifecycle tests. For return or destruction, match the stated trigger exactly: termination or expiration supports a termination-triggered duty, while request, demand, or the end of discussions alone does not. For retention, inspect the disposition command and all express archival, backup, legal-record, or dispute exceptions; an all-information-and-copies command without such an exception supports the opposed boundary. For survival, require obligations expressly continuing after termination, rather than a fixed term, antecedent-breach liability, or a disposition clause. Cite the trigger, disposition scope, responsive exception, and continuation language only; do not borrow evidence between the three tests.

Test employee disclosure, outsider disclosure, and copying separately. For each, match the receiving actor, action, recipient class, quantifier, and every condition. A general third-party prohibition with an employee exception may permit employee access while opposing outsider permission; permission for consultants, agents, advisers, contractors, or affiliates does not automatically answer the employee proposition. Discretionary written consent alone is not standing permission. For copying, a necessity- or purpose-limited exception permits some copying, whereas an absolute or consent-only prohibition opposes it. Cite the operative rule and all fragments supplying recipient class or conditions; include independently responsive repetitions, but exclude general safeguards, recipient liability, use limits, headings, and adjacent classes. Absence of permission is not itself opposition.

Find the operative exclusion or permission lead-in first, then attach only the responsive continuation. Independent development must be without use of, reference to, or access to protected information. Third-party acquisition requires an external source entitled to disclose and, when stated, free of a confidentiality duty; public-domain and prior-possession provisions are not substitutes. Treat compelled-disclosure authority and notice as separate questions: verify legal compulsion, whether notice is required or excused, protective-order opportunity, and any required-portion limit. Cite the lead-in whenever it supplies scope and every fragment completing the responsive subparagraph; exclude headings and neighboring exceptions. If no matching exception exists, do not infer its opposite.

Match the regulated actor, modality, direct conduct, protected object or people, duration, and exceptions. Reverse engineering requires express reverse-engineer, decompile, disassemble, decrypt, decipher, reconstruct, re-identify, or materially equivalent conduct directed at protected material or an embodying product; a heading alone is insufficient, and copying, confidentiality, ownership, return, signature, or severability text is not a substitute. Solicitation requires recruiting, soliciting, inducing departure, hiring, or comparable conduct directed at the specified representatives; a restriction concerning only customers or business opportunities does not establish it. Cite every fragment completing the actor and restriction. If the direct conduct is absent, use absence rather than inventing an opposing permission.

Test rights and agreement secrecy separately. No-license requires operative language that no license, right, title, interest, option, or other right is granted or implied; ownership, restricted use, access, or a disclaimer alone is insufficient. Agreement confidentiality requires protection of the agreement's existence or terms, or of the fact, status, or substance of negotiations or discussions; an entire-agreement clause or ordinary confidentiality of disclosed information is not responsive. Cite every fragment carrying the protected subject and prohibition, excluding headings, signatures, purpose clauses, and neighboring ownership or use text.

Find every independently operative restriction limiting use of protected information to the agreement's stated purpose. Match the regulated actor, protected object, allowed purpose, and any clause that defines or independently restates that purpose. A disclosure rule, confidentiality duty, ownership clause, copy restriction, recital, or permission to receive information is not itself a use limitation. Cite all responsive repeated operative provisions, even when one is already sufficient, while excluding headings, recipient-class clauses, and adjacent restrictions that merely help interpretation.

Read every operative definition as one logical chain. Test breadth first: technical-only coverage requires a closed protected class confined to technical subject matter; any alternative covering business, financial, commercial, customer, personnel, marketing, or other information opposes exclusivity. Test identification separately: every route into the protected class must depend on the discloser’s marking or designation; an alternative based on nature, context, reasonable expectation, or confidentiality regardless of labeling opposes universal express identification. Oral or visual coverage supports verbal inclusion even when subject to contemporaneous designation or later written confirmation. Cite every fragment supplying an alternative route or condition and independently operative repeated definitions; exclude headings, recitals, exclusions, and adjacent examples that do not establish scope.

complete_original_evidence_texts: 1. Confidential Information means:

(i) technologies in written or tangible form disclosed to COMPANY from time to time after the Effective Date of this Agreement by ROCHESTER and identified with particularity at time of disclosure and marked confidential; and

(ii) technologies communicated orally or visually to COMPANY by ROCHESTER, if it is reduced to writing or other tangible form by ROCHESTER on or before the date thirty days after the date of such communication, marked confidential, and promptly delivered to COMPANY.

Confidential information also includes any information of the owner and a third party with which the Owner deals, including, but not limited to: financial information, business records, plans, trade secrets, product ideas, technical data of any type, contracts, billing records, pricing structure, discounts, property, investments, strategic alliances, partnerships, customer or client lists.
The nature of the information and manner of the disclosure are such that a reasonable person would understand to be confidential.

“Confidential Information” includes all business, financial, contractual, marketing and/or technical information, in whatever form embodied, which has been or may be disclosed, or to which access is provided, by a party (“Discloser”) to the other party to this Agreement (“Recipient”), which
(a) if in writing, is marked “confidential”, “proprietary” or other similar marking at the time of disclosure, or
(b) if provided orally or visually, is identified as confidential at the time of disclosure and confirmed in writing to Recipient within 15 days of such disclosure.

In this deed, the term Confidential Information means any and all information disclosed by NostraData to the Confidant in any form (including verbally, electronically, visually, in writing or in any other tangible form, and all copies of any such information), which is identified as, notified as being, or which would be reasonably expected to be, confidential or proprietary to NostraData.
